Summary: The paper proposes CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that certifies, with finite-sample confidence 1-δ, that an influence-weighted answered-set error rate averaged over the population of sites is at most α, treating the site (hospital) rather than the record as the unit of independence. Each calibration site is collapsed to a bounded atom Z_c (with a data-independent influence cap M=100), a Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting martingale tests E[Z] ≥ α, and a fixed-sequence (learn-then-test style) walk over a 23-point threshold grid, ordered on a disjoint auxiliary split, selects the operating threshold. Two assumption modes are offered: an exchangeable baseline and a BBSE label-shift mode whose four estimated parameters (c0, c1, π_source, q_target) carry a Bonferroni-split cluster-bootstrap/Clopper-Pearson uncertainty box tested at both ρ endpoints. An L2-logistic head yields exact additive attributions for answers and abstentions, and a three-way answered-set composition disclosure is reported alongside the certificate. Validation comprises a 208-site synthetic grid (E1 validity, E2 label shift, E3 concept-shift negative control, E4 site-count frontier, E5 explanations, E6 per-site coverage/composition, E7 record-as-unit comparator, plus an M-sensitivity sweep) and an eICU-CRD v2.0 study (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol committed before the extract was read: α=0.10 certifies on all 20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 mean coverage, α=0.05 on none, BBSE certifies nothing, and the answered set's mortality (0.046) is about half the pool's (0.090).
Strengths: The problem framing is correct and important: multi-site clinical deployment does break record-level exchangeability, and making the site the atom of a finite-sample selective-risk certificate is the right first-order fix; the martingale argument for the exchangeable mode (bounded atoms, predictable capped bets, Ville's inequality) is standard and appears sound.

The estimand is stated precisely and its limits (site-population average, not per-site; parameter not realized count; concept shift out of scope; joint 1-2δ over the α ladder) are written into a frozen guarantee text; the paper is unusually candid about what the certificate does not promise.

The validation harness is more careful than most: an oracle synthetic generator, a concept-shift negative control that is verified to be poisonous before it is used, a record-as-unit comparator on identical draws, an influence-cap sensitivity sweep, and a real-data protocol with pre-declared predictions and failure criteria (including three falsified predictions reported as such).

The eICU study is executed responsibly: attrition ledger with deaths at every step, deny-by-default feature allowlist and leak denylist, pre-registered leak screens (one of which fired in the opposite direction and is reported honestly), an external clinical comparator (APACHE-IVa), and aggregate-only release under the DUA.
Full code release with deterministic, byte-identical regeneration of the synthetic grid and pinned constants is a genuine reproducibility asset.
Weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty for an ML venue: the core is a straightforward composition of known pieces (WSR betting on per-cluster bounded means, fixed-sequence/LTT threshold selection, BBSE with a Bonferroni parameter box in the style of Si et al., closed-form linear attributions). Cluster-as-unit distribution-free inference (Dunn et al.; Lee et al.) and label-shift uncertainty propagation already exist; the delta is engineering and disclosure discipline rather than a new statistical idea. Contributions 3 and 4 (exact attributions for a linear model; a negative control that can fail) are good practice, not contributions.

The label-shift mode is a non-result empirically. In E2 it declines all 200 draws at every non-null shift magnitude and certifies only 9% at the null; on eICU it fits (ρ̂=0.668, box [0.068, 1.986]) and certifies nothing. No experiment shows BBSE certifying under an actual shift, so 'label-shift robustness' in the title reduces to 'declines instead of overclaiming'. Moreover, three of the four BBSE intervals are asymptotic percentile bootstraps with measured joint miscoverage 0.038 vs nominal ≤0.019, so the 'finite-sample' claim holds only for the exchangeable mode.

The certified guarantee at realistic scale is close to trivial in clinical terms. At ~9% prevalence with a symmetric 0-1 loss, α=0.10 is the only reachable rung at 74-83 calibration clusters, and the paper's own numbers show the eICU answered set has mortality 0.046, the head's answered error is 0.042, and its skill margin over an always-negative rule on the answered set is 0.0039 (answered-minus-all contrast negative). The certificate is met largely by abstaining where deaths concentrate; the authors disclose this, but it undercuts the practical significance of the certified number. α=0.05 needs 300-400 sites, which essentially no clinical consortium has.

No comparison against alternative valid cluster-aware certification procedures. The only comparator is the authors' own record-as-unit variant. Whether WSR betting on site atoms is materially tighter than, e.g., an empirical-Bernstein/Hoeffding bound on the same atoms, a cluster-bootstrap CI, or hierarchical/non-exchangeable conformal risk control (Dunn et al.; Farinhas et al.) is never shown, so the claim that the α frontier is 'a property of how many hospitals one has, not of the method' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The E7 motivating-failure demonstration is weaker than framed: at the base heterogeneity (s_u=0.5) the record-unit certifier's aggregate violation rate is 3.5%, i.e., inside δ; the ~2δ violation appears only at s_u=2.0. At α=0.10 the record-unit comparator does not violate at all (fresh-pool risk 0.081). The comparator is also run on an arbitrary 2,000-record subsample of S_cal without justification of that size.

E1's validity check is unstressed: mean fresh-pool R_M is 0.057 against α=0.10, so 0/200 exceedances mostly reflects a loose bound (the information floor at ~80 clusters is ~0.035) rather than a tight δ-level test. There is no arm where the true answered risk sits near α, which is where a validity claim would actually be tested.

The synthetic generator is favorable to the method (d=8, linear signal on 4 features, logistic head is the correct model class, heterogeneity only via a Gaussian site random effect on the outcome log-odds); generalization of the empirical findings to nonlinear heads or richer between-site case-mix shift is untested. E5 returns a null on the synthetic arm.

Real-data evidence is a single cohort with 20 re-splits of one hospital population, which by the authors' own admission bounds gross violation but cannot estimate the violation rate; only two α rungs are ever considered.

Presentation: the manuscript is long, dense, and repetitive (the site-population-average caveat is restated many times), leans on rhetorical framing ('honest', 'the system working rather than failing', 'stated rather than patched over'), and reports many quantities to 5-6 decimal places (0.002914, 0.035948, 0.000975) that carry no meaning. Key technical content needed to check soundness (the BBSE-reweighted atom's boundedness and affinity in ρ, the anti-conservative truncation counterexample, the four-step martingale argument) is deferred to a supplement not included.
Questions: Under BBSE reweighting, please state the per-site atom explicitly. Is it still bounded in [0,1] for every ρ in the box, and is the quantity whose sign decides certification exactly affine in ρ (so that testing the two endpoints suffices)? How is normalization handled when the class weights depend on ρ?

How does the WSR betting test on site atoms compare, at 74-83 calibration clusters, with simpler valid alternatives on the same atoms (Hoeffding, empirical Bernstein, a cluster-bootstrap or t-based CI on the mean of Z_c) and with hierarchical/non-exchangeable conformal risk control? Is the α=0.05 frontier at 300-400 sites a property of the betting test's constants or of any valid procedure?

Is there any configuration, synthetic or real, in which the BBSE mode certifies under a genuine non-null prevalence shift? What target-pool size and number of declared target sites would be required for the box to become narrow enough?

In E7, why is the record-as-unit comparator run on a 2,000-record subsample of S_cal rather than all calibration records? How do its certify and violation rates change on the full record set at both heterogeneity levels?

Can you add a validity stress arm where the true answered-set risk is near α (e.g., a generator tuned so R_M ≈ 0.09 at the deployed threshold) so that the observed exceedance rate can be compared meaningfully against δ, rather than 0/200 at R_M ≈ 0.057?

On eICU the answered-set skill margin over an always-negative rule is 0.0039 and the answered-minus-all contrast is negative. What is the clinical value of an α=0.10 symmetric-error certificate on an answered set with 4.6% mortality? Is a certificate on the answered-set false-negative rate (or a cost-weighted atom) feasible at this cluster count, and if not, what does that imply for the method's applicability?
Given the BBSE box's asymptotic bootstrap intervals with measured under-coverage, will the title/abstract restrict the 'finite-sample' claim to the exchangeable mode?
Were the eICU split proportions (24 held-out hospitals; 73/36/74) and the number of re-splits pre-registered, and how sensitive are the certified τ* and coverage to them?
Limitations: The authors are thorough about limitations: site-population average rather than per-site bound (with individual hospitals observed at 0.29 answered error under a certificate whose pools average 0.048); concept shift excluded; BBSE intervals asymptotic with measured under-coverage; symmetric loss with ~77% of answered errors being false negatives; single real cohort with 20 re-splits of one population; temporal common-shock correlation unmodeled; only the influence cap swept; git-commit pre-registration weaker than a third-party registry.

Not adequately addressed: the practical near-triviality of the α=0.10 rung at ~9% prevalence (the only rung reachable at realistic site counts) and the absence of any regime where the label-shift mode certifies; the missing comparison to alternative valid cluster-aware bounds, which leaves the tightness of the chosen test uncharacterized.

Potential negative societal impact: a 'certified' label on a gate whose answered set is enriched for survivors could give deployers false reassurance about performance on the deaths that matter clinically; the composition disclosure mitigates this only if deployers read it. Equity across hospitals is not guaranteed by the certificate (dispersion is measured, not bounded).
